title: Week 11: Using rjags for MCMC, diagnosing convergence
text:
\(\renewcommand{\text}[1]{\textsf{#1}}\)
In the Wednesday lecture, we introduce the Metropolis-Hastings-algorithm (“MH”). We start with the general principle and an example for its implementation. The algorithm has an interesting history; if time allows, we will also touch upon that. Then we discuss variants of MH-sampling: we will see that using a symmetric proposal density makes calculations a bit simpler. One can also combine Gibbs sampling with MH, which is important in Bayesian analysis for multivariate parameters, when the priors are not conjugate to the likelihood.
All these algorithms can be used ``out of the box’’; there are various software options. You will learn to use the software JAGS for Bayesian data analysis. To this end, you need to describe your model in a well defined way; I will discuss the general structure of JAGS model descriptions and we look at a few examples. You can download the JAGS user manual here and on brightspace.
Finally, we look at statistics that help to assess if the Markov chains have converged and are mixing well: trace plots, the Geweke and Gelman statistics. The effective sample size tells us how much information we get out of a long Markov chain as compared to independent sampling. This is usually less, due to autocorrelation. We will discuss points to consider if we want to improve convergence speed and decrease autocorrelation (R&G, Section 3.4.2, 3.4.3).

title: Week 7: Models for over- and underdispersed counts, and model validation by AIC
text:
\(\renewcommand{\text}[1]{\textsf{#1}}\)
The main topic of this week are slightly advanced models for count data, and model assessment. As time allows, we will also treat some “loose ends”, such as the Fisher scoring method behind the glm function, and more background on contingency tables and the Poisson trick.
The Poisson model is a good start for count data. Sometimes, however, there is more variation in the data than we would expect under a Poisson model. This is called overdispersion. One reason for overdispersion is that the population is composed of subpopulations with different mean. We will learn about the negative binomial distribution as a mixture of Poisson distributions. Another reason for overdispersion is zero-inflation: there are more “0”s in the data than we would expect under the models in question.
A very popular general tool for assessment of model fit is Akaike’s information criterion (AIC). You will apply this to glms, and learn about its theoretical background: it is related to the mean Kullback-Leibler divergence between the “true” distribution and all fitted distributions from a family.

Problem 7.2: Homicides
(based on Agresti, problem 7.31)
Table 7.5. in Agresti(2015), shown below, summarizes responses of 1308 subjects to the question: within the past 12 months, how many people have you known personally that were victims of homicide?
The table shows responses by race, for those who identified their race as white or as black. You can download the data homicides.csv here or find it in thedata folder on Google Drive.

Problem 7.3: The index of dispersion test
For i.i.d. samples \(\boldsymbol{Y}=(Y_1,\dots, Y_n)\), the index of dispersion is defined as \[
D(\boldsymbol{Y}) = \frac{S^2}{\overline{Y}}, \ \text{where}\  \overline{Y}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i,\ \ S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \overline{Y})^2.
\]
If the sample comes from a Poisson distribution, the expectation of the numerator is the same as the expectation of the denominator. Therefore, values close to 1 suggest Poisson distribution, while values larger than 1 indicate overdispersion and values less than 1 indicate underdispersion.
Under the Poisson assumption, \((n-1)D(\boldsymbol{Y})\) is approximately \(\chi^2\) distributed with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom. This can be used to construct an approximate test for the hypothesis that the data stem from a Poisson distribution. A popular rule of thumb tells that the approximation is good, when the mean of \(Y\) is larger than 5 (in the literature, this is commonly called \(m>5\)), even when the sample size \(n\) is small.

The rule of thumb is apparently due to Hoel (1943)1, who studied the quality of the \(\chi^2\) approximation by numerical calculations. He looked at various combination of theoretical mean \(m\) and sample size \(n\), and concluded that the test becomes slightly conservative if \(m \leq 2\).
Conduct a simulation experiment to check Hoel’s findings: estimate the true rejection rate of a \(\chi^2\) based index of dispersion test, for \(m \in\{1, 2, 5, 25\}\) and \(n\in\{3, 5, 10, 25\}\).

Hints

to estimate the rejection rate, find the critical values of the \(\chi^2\) distribution. For a two-sided test that is sensitive to both over- and underdispersion, reject the null hypothesis if \(D\) is smaller than the \(\alpha/2\)- quantile or larger than the \((1-\alpha/2)\)-quantile of the \(\chi^2\) distribution.
An R hint for fast generation of (nrep) realizations of \(D\):

Y <- matrix(rpois(n * nrep, m), nrow = n)
D <- apply(Y, 2, var) / apply(Y, 2, mean)   




Use the index of dispersion test to check if the Poisson model is appropriate for the data from the previous exercise about homicides (Agresti, Table 7.5). Treat black and white persons as separate samples from possibly different Poisson distributions.




Problem 7.4: Simulation based model tests

Consider Exercise 6.3, “A graphical model check” from last week. You can turn this “gut feeling” into a test with well defined rejection rate \(\alpha = 0.05\) by simulating 19 realizations, and arranging them on a grid together with the one observed plot at a random position within the 20 plots. Then ask an impartial judge (e.g. your grandmother) to point out the most unusual plot – this test rejects the null hypothesis if the judge pointed at the plot made from the actual data. One problem here is that the test may be conservative because you test the fitted model. But for a given model, the size of this test is equal to \(\alpha\).
Discuss why this is a test of size \(\alpha\) for a given model. What is \(\alpha\) if you only simulate 9 plots?

R hint
In Problem 6.3 you were asked to compare scatterplots of the crabs data with scatterplots of simulated data from the fitted model. Here is one way to solve this.
We make the scatterplot with transparent dots to make multiplicity of observations visible. adjustcolor is an easy way to define transparent colors

 crabs <- read.csv("./data/crabs.csv")
 transparentblue <- adjustcolor("blue",  alpha = 0.2)           
 plot(y ~ weight, data = crabs, pch = 16, col = transparentblue)








The R function simulate simulates response values from a fitted model. It returns a data.frame where each column corresponds to one simulation. If you do not specify the argument nsim, it will just simulate one realization.

 # fit model
 fitted <- glm(y ~ weight, data= crabs, family = poisson)
 # make 4 simulations from fitted model and plot
 new_y <- simulate(fitted)
 plot(new_y[,1] ~ weight, data = crabs, pch = 16, col = transparentblue, ylab = "y")

title: Week 5 : general results and methods for glm
text:
\(\renewcommand{\text}[1]{\textsf{#1}}\)
How do we estimate parameters in a generalized linear models? How do we test hypotheses about the parameters?
You will fit glms to data, using R’s function glm. You will learn about the theoretical background, maximum likelihood estimation in glms. We will also have a look at the asymptotic properties of MLE in the context of glm. If time allows, we discuss numerical techniques behind solving the maximum likelihood equations, in particular iterative reweighted least squares. The second lecture deals with model assessment. Goodness of fit of glm can be assessed by the deviance – a likelihood ratio statistic (👍) – or by studying residuals. We will also see how to estimate the dispersion parameter in situations where it is not given.

Problem 5.1: GLM for comparing two groups
(Compare Agresti 2015, Exercises 4.6 and 4.7)
In this exercise we consider data from two groups \(A\) and \(B\) of size \(n_A\) and \(n_B\), that can be modelled by i.i.d. Poisson variables within each group (thus we have in all a sample of size \(n=n_A +n_B\)). The first \(n_A\) observations belong to a group \(A\), and the remaining \(n_B\) belong to a group \(B\), with different group means \(\mu_A\) and \(\mu_B\). For the analysis by a GLM, we use the linear predictor \(g(\mu_i) = \eta_i=\beta_0 +\beta_1 \mathbf{1}(i \in \{1,..., n_A\} )\).

Show that for the log-link function, the GLM likelihood equations imply that the fitted means \(\hat\mu_A\) and \(\hat\mu_B\) equal the sample means.
Show that the result of a) holds no matter what link function \(g\) is used or what exponential dispersion family distribution for the \(Y_i\) is assumed.

You could also try to generalize the result to more than two groups.

Problem 5.2: Survival times
Times to event (survival times) are often modeled by an exponential distribution. Recall that this is a special case of Gamma distribution :-)
The following data example deals with survival data of leukemia patients and is a classic . Here \(y_i\) represent times to death in weeks from diagnosis, and \(x_i\) the \(\log_{10}\) of initial white blood cell count, for seventeen patients.
The R code below generates vectors y and x:

y <- c(65, 156, 100, 134, 16, 108, 121, 4, 39, 143, 56, 26, 22, 1, 1, 5, 65)
x <- c(3.36, 2.88, 3.63, 3.41, 3.78, 4.02, 4.00, 4.23, 3.73, 3.85, 3.97, 4.51, 
       4.54, 5.00, 5.00, 4.72, 5.00)

A possible specification for \(\mathrm{E}\,{y_i}\) is \[
  \mathrm{E}\,(y_i) = \exp(\beta_1+ \beta_2 x_i),
  \] which will ensure that \(\mathrm{E}\,(y)\) is non-negative for all values of the parameters and all values of \(x\). Which link function is appropriate in this case?
Using R’s function glm, fit a model that assumes that the \(y_i\) have an exponential distribution, with mean \(\mathrm{E}\,(y_i)\) given in (b). Hint: use the Gamma family. The Gamma shape parameter has no influence on the estimate of the model parameters in a glm.
For the fitted model, compare the observed values \(y_i\) and fitted values \(\hat{y}_i=\exp(\hat\beta_1+ \hat\beta_2 x_i)\), and use the standardized residuals \(r_i = (y_i-\hat{y}_i)/\hat{y_i}\) to investigate the adequacy of the model.  (Note: \(\hat{y_i}\) is used as the denominator of \(r_i\) because it is an estimate of the standard deviation of \(y_i\)— why is this?)

Problem 5.4: Deviance goodness of fit test for the Poisson model - when does asymptotic theory work, and when not?
In the lectures, we have learned that the scaled deviance can be used to test if a model describes the data well, since scaled deviance between a model and the corresponding saturated model often has an asymptotic \(\chi^2\)-distribution. In this exercise, you explore this for a Poisson model by simulation.
Let \(Y_1,\dots, Y_n\) be independent Poisson distributed variables with \(\mathrm{E}\,Y_i = \lambda_i\). This is the saturated model \(M_0\). In the submodel \(M_1\), all mean values coincide, that is, \(\lambda_1=\dots=\lambda_n\).

Show that the scaled deviance for model \(M_1\) is given as \[
D=2\sum_{j=1}^n Y_j\log\left(\frac{Y_j}{\bar{Y}}\right),\quad\bar{Y}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i,
\]
where we set \(Y_j\log(Y_j/\bar{Y}) = 0\) if \(Y_j=0\).
Extra (ad libitum): show that \(\lim\limits_{x\to 0} x \log(x) = 0\).
Simulate \(N=1000\) values of \(D\) and compare with a \(\chi^2\)-distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom. For a visual comparison, you can for example use an appropriate qq-plot (not qqnorm). Also estimate the probability that \(D\) exceeds the \(95\%\)-quantile of the \(\chi^2_{n-1}\)-distribution.
Do this for several values of \(\lambda\) and \(n\), e.g. \(\lambda = 1, 10, 100\) and \(n=10, 100, 1000\). In some cases, you will observe that the \(\chi^2\)-approximation is not good. Summarize your findings - when would you recommend a goodness-of-fit test based on the \(\chi^2\)-approximation of the scaled deviance, and when not?
Try to explain your findings.

title: Week 3: Asymptotics, Likelihood Ratio Statistics, Delta Method and Generating Functions
text:
\(\renewcommand{\text}[1]{\textsf{#1}}\)
We will finish the topic on likelihood theory with a proof of asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator, and a short discussion of likelihood ratio statistics. Very related to the use of asymptotic normality is the so called delta method that allows us to approximate the variance of a transformed random variable - this method will also be discussed.
In order to be prepared for the next big topic, generalized linear models, please recall the fundamentals of normal linear models. Exercises 3 will contain a problem about linear models.
Generalized linear models apply to random variables that have a distribution belonging to the so called exponential dispersion family. This class of distributions has some useful theoretical properties in common. Very handy tool to prove these properties (and a lot more) are the moment generating function and the related cumulant generating function. When we have finished likelihood theory, we will look at generating functions.

Suppose that \(X_1,\dots,X_n \ {\stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim }}\ \mathrm{Gamma}(r,\lambda)\).

Find the variance of \(\bar{X}\).
Use the delta method to find the approximate variance of \(\overline{X}^2\).

(see MSRR1, Exercise 13.5)

Problem 3.3: Approximate confidence interval for a ratio
This is an exercise where you apply the delta method for two independent random variables. How to do that is described in Davison, p.34 f., in particular Example 2.25.
One application where the delta method is particularly helpful is when you need a good guess for the variance of a ratio (Davison, Example 2.25). An example where the ratio was interesting is known from the book that we used in the course “Mathematical Statistics”, MSRR1: there, the suspicion was raised that the telecom giant Verizon delays the repair times for customers from competing local carriers (CLEC) in relation to own customers (ILEC). To express this, we are interested in the ratio of the mean repair times for CLEC and ILEC customers.
When dealing with ratios, it is often advised to look at the logarithm of the ratio instead. One reason is that this statistic is symmetric. In the current exercise, you consider both the ratio and the log ratio. We estimate the ratio of (population) means by the ratio of sample means. This estimator is not unbiased (why?), but the bias is small if the variance of the denominator is small.
Start with theoretical calculations:

Let \(X_1,\dots, X_n\) and \(Y_1,\dots, Y_m\) be independent random variables with means \(\mu_X\) and \(\mu_Y\) and variances \(\sigma^2_X\) and \(\sigma^2_Y\), respectively.
Show that the delta method gives approximate variances \[\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{Var}\,\left[\frac{\overline{X}}{\overline{Y}}\right] \approx
\frac{\sigma_X^2}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{\mu_Y^2} + \frac{\sigma_Y^2}{m}\cdot\frac{\mu_X^2}{\mu_Y^4}
\end{equation*}\] and \[\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{Var}\,\left[\log\left(\frac{\overline{X}}{\overline{Y}}\right)\right] \approx
\frac{\sigma_X^2}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{\mu_X^2} + \frac{\sigma_Y^2}{m}\cdot\frac{1}{\mu_Y^2}.
\end{equation*}\]

Then apply these results to the Verizon data. You can find them in the R-package resampledata3 or alternatively download Verizon.csv directly or find it on the data folder on Google Drive.

Calculate the approximate means and variances of ratio and log ratio from the data, where \(X\) stands for the CLEC (\(n=23\) repair times) and \(Y\) for the ILEC (these were \(m=1664\) repair times). To this end replace theoretical mean and variance by the sample mean and variance of the data.
Use the means and variances from part (b) to calculate an approximate 95% confidence interval for the ratio of means, based on normal approximation. Transform the confidence interval for the log ratio into a confidence interval for the original ratio. Comment on your results.
(optional) Use bootstrap to estimate the variances of \(\overline{X}/\overline{Y}\) and \(\log(\overline{X}/\overline{Y})\) for the Verizon data. Compare with your results from the delta method in (b).

(Inspired by MSRR1, Exercises 13.6, 13.7 and 13.8)


The last exercise is meant as a refresher on normal linear models in preparation for the coming module on generalized linear models (glms). You can read more on normal linear models in Chapter 8 of Davison(2003). Sections 8.1 - 8.5 cover mainly the topic as taught from the course “Mathematical Statistics”, see Chapter 11 of the course notes from 2024 (Davison gives slightly more advanced details). I suggest that you first read Exercise 4 and if you can solve it without major problems you are good to go for glms. Otherwise glance through the first sections of Chapter 8 in Davison, or Section 11.1 in the course notes. The course notes also contain useful R-codes and recipes for specifying model formulas in R. Find a brief overview in the extra onenote notes review-linear-models.pdf.

Problem 3.4: Interpretation of estimated parameters in an “analysis of covariance” model
For 72 young girls suffering from anorexia, the Anorexia.csv file that you can download from the data folder on Google Drive shows their weights before and after an experimental period. The girls were randomly assigned to receive one of three therapies during this period. A control group received the standard therapy, which was compared to family therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy. Download the data and fit a linear model relating the weight after the experimental period to the initial weight and the therapy.

title: Week 1: Introduction, Likelihood theory
text:
\(\renewcommand{\text}[1]{\textsf{#1}}\)
The first week is devoted to general topics around likelihood. We start with recapitulating likelihood and a bit of likelihood theory. Some things that may be new to you include relative likelihood, as well as observed and expected information (aka Fisher information), which is crucial for statistical inference on the models.
Then we state the asymptotic properties of maximum likelihood estimators (mle) in so-called regular models, that is models where the distribution fulfills certain conditions. In these cases, it is possible to give approximate confidence intervals and statistical tests based on normality, the so-called Wald intervals and Wald tests.
We will see what is behind this theory next week. In order to get there, we need to know what “asymptotically” means, and remind us of (or introduce) modes of stochastic convergence, and connections between them.

Exercises 1

Remember: exercise classes (TØ) start in course week 2. Please try to solve at least some of the problems before you come to the TØ 😊🧐.

Problem 1.1: relative likelihood in the binomial model
We have seen that relative likelihood can be used to judge how well a model with a given parameter is supported by the data, see (4.11) in Davison (p. 100). In this exercise, you compare this measure of goodness of fit with good old p-values in a simple situation.
Consider the binomial model with size parameter \(n=20\), and probability parameter \(\theta\in (0,1)\). We have observed data consisting of one realization, \(y=4\).

Write down the relative likelihood for this model and the given data.
Calculate \(RL(\theta)\) for \(\theta=0.01, 0.02,\dots, 0.99\) and find out which values of \(\theta\) are supported by the data according to the table in (4.11) (strongly, weakly, poorly, very poorly). You can use R or any other programming language of your choice for this.
Calculate the \(p\)-values of a twosided test for \(\theta = \theta_0\) where \(\theta_0=0.01, 0.02,\dots, 0.99\). In R, you can use function prop.test. Compare with the results of part (b).
Try with other values \(n\) and \(y\), or even with other distributions (optional).




Problem 1.2: observed and expected information: gamma distribution
Davison, Exercise 4.3.1
The gamma distribution with scale parameter \(\lambda\) and shape parameter \(\kappa\) has probability density function (see eq. (2.7) in Davison, p. 23)
\[
f(y; \lambda, \kappa) = \frac{\lambda^\kappa y^{\kappa-1}}{\Gamma(\kappa)}\exp(-\lambda y),\quad y>0,\ \ \lambda,\kappa>0.
\] This distribution has mean \(\kappa/\lambda\) and variance \(\kappa/\lambda^2\).
a) Show that the log likelihood for a random sample from density of the Gamma distribution is
\[
\ell(\lambda, \kappa)= n\kappa\log\lambda + (\kappa -1)\sum_{j=1}^n \log y_j .
- \lambda\sum_{j=1}^n y_j - n\log\Gamma(\kappa).
\] Deduce that the observed information is \[
J(\lambda,\kappa)= n\begin{pmatrix}
\kappa/\lambda^2 & -1/\lambda\\
-1/\lambda& \mathrm{d}^2\log \Gamma(\kappa)/\mathrm{d}\kappa^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\] and find the expected information \(I(\lambda,\kappa)\).
b) Suppose that we write \(\lambda=\kappa/\mu\), where \(\mu\) is the distribution mean. Find the log likelihood in terms of \(\mu\) and \(\kappa\), and show that \(J(\mu,\kappa)\) is random and that
\[I(\mu, \kappa)=n\,\mathrm{diag}(2\kappa/\mu^2, \mathrm{d}^2\log\Gamma(\kappa)/\mathrm{d}\kappa^2-1/\kappa).
\]



Problem 1.3: Fisher information and relative efficiency: geometric distribution
Davison, Exercise 4.3.5
Find the expected information for \(\theta\) based on a random sample \(Y_1,\dots, Y_n\) from the geometric density
\[
  f(y;\theta)=\theta(1-\theta)^{y-1},\quad y=1,2,3,\dots, \ \ 0<\theta<1.
\] 🤔 A statistician has a choice between observing random samples from the Bernoulli or geometric densities with the same \(\theta\). Which will give the more precise inference on \(\theta\)?



Problem 1.4: using the theory in a practical example
Davison, R practical 4.2. (find the practicals on BrightSpace under General Information \(\to\) Textbooks)

To get the data into R, install package SMPracticals. The code given in the practical then runs out of the box if you replace data(births) by attach(SMPracticals::births). Just to practice good habits, remember to clean up the environment by detach(SMPracticals::births) when you are done with the calculations.
In the code provided you will see that they make use of the Hessian matrix coming with the optimization by function nlm.
If you never came across the notion of a Hessian matrix, read about it e.g. on Wikipedia - it is just a matrix of second derivatives, but here it is very useful. 



Problem 1.5: information in a model for survival times
Davison, 4.9: Problem 6
Persons who catch an infectious disease either die almost at once during its initial phase, or live an exponential time; denote the survival time \(Y\) and declare that \(Y = 0\) if death occurs in the initial phase. Explain why the likelihood can be written as a product of terms of form
\[
(1-p)^{1-I} \times \{p/\theta\,\exp(-Y/\theta)\}^I,\quad 0<p<1,\ \ \theta>0,
\] where \(I\) is an indicator of survival beyond the initial phase. Give interpretations of \(p\) and \(\theta\).
Given data \((i_1, y_1),\dots,(i_n,y_n)\) on the survival of \(n\) persons, show that the log likelihood has form
\[
\ell(p,\theta) = r \log p + (n-r)\log(1-p) - r\log\theta - \frac{1}{\theta}\sum_{j=1}^n i_j y_j,
\] where \(r=\sum_{j=1}^n i_j\), and hence find the maximum likelihood estimators of \(p\) and \(\theta\), together with the observed and expected information matrices.
Comment on the form of the information matrices and give approximate 95% confidence intervals for the parameters.

title: Week 2: stochastic convergence and properties of mle
text:
\(\renewcommand{\text}[1]{\textsf{#1}}\)
We will continue with modes of stochastic convergence, recall the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem as examples, and see how these modes of convergence relate to each other.
Under certain conditions, the maximum likelihood estimator (mle) is consistent and asymptotically normal distributed. In context with the proof of consistency of mle we will shortly come across the Kullback-Leibler-divergence, a way to characterize the distance between two distributions that which will be important later in the course.
On the way to proving the asymptotic normality of MLE, we will take a closer look at the score function \(U(\theta; \boldsymbol{Y})\), and derive Bartlett’s identities about the mean and variance of \(U(\theta;\boldsymbol{Y})\).

Exercises 2

You need not have solved all problems before the exercise class. However to get most out of the class, read the problems thoroughly and try at least some of them before the theoretical exercises.




Tricking MathJax with invisible \(a^2+b^2\)


Problem 2.1: Convergence of the product of two sample means
Davison(2003), Section 2.2: Exercise 4 (slightly extended)
Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) and \(Y_1,\dots, Y_n\) be independent random samples from the exponential densities \(f_X =\lambda\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x},\ x>0\) and \(f_Y(y) =\lambda^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-y/\lambda},\ y>0\), with \(\lambda>0\). Let \(\overline{X}\) and \(\overline{Y}\) denote the sample averages.

Show that \(\overline{X} \overline{Y}\xrightarrow{P} 1\) as \(n\to\infty\).
Write a simulation to illustrate the result in a). You can do this even if you don’t think you succeeded with a formal proof; use a programming language of your choice.




Problem 2.2: Maximum likelihood and information in a linear model
Davison (2003) Section 4.9: Problem 10.
In a normal linear model through the origin, independent observations \(Y_1,\dots, Y_n\) are such that \(Y_j\sim N(\beta x_j, \sigma^2)\).
Show that the log likelihood for a sample \(y_1,\dots, y_n\) is
\[
\ell(\beta, \sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^n(y_j-\beta x_j)^2.
\]
Deduce that the likelihood equations are equivalent to \(\sum x_j(y_j-\hat\beta x_j)=0\) and \(\hat{\sigma^2}=n^{-1}\sum (y_j-\hat\beta{x_j})^2\), and hence find the maximum likelihood estimates \(\hat{\beta}\) and \(\hat{\sigma^2}\) for data with \(x=(1,2,3,4,5)\) and \(y = (2.81, 5.48, 7.11, 8.69, 11.28)\).
Show that the observed information matrix evaluated at the maximum likelihood estimates is diagonal and use it to obtain approximate 95% confidence intervals for the parameters. Plot the data and your fitted line \(y =\hat{\beta} x\). Say whether you think the model is correct, with reasons. Discuss the adequacy of the normal approximations in this example.


Three small exercises covering facts and examples for convergence in probability:




Tricking MathJax with invisible \(a^2+b^2\)


Problem 2.3: Continuous mapping theorem, version for convergence in probability
Davison (2003) Section 2.2, Exercise 1.
Suppose that \(S_n\xrightarrow{P} s_0\), and that the function \(h\) is continuous at \(s_0\), that is, for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists a \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-y|<\delta\) implies that \(|h(x)-h(y)|<\varepsilon\). Explain why this implies that
\[\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{P}(|S_n-s_0|<\delta) \leq \mathrm{P}(|h(S_n)-h(s_0)|<\varepsilon) \leq 1,
\end{equation*}\]
and deduce that \(\mathrm{P}(|h(S_n)-h(s_0)|<\varepsilon) \longrightarrow 1\) as \(n\to\infty\). That is, \(h(S_n)\xrightarrow{P}h(s_0)\).






Tricking MathJax with invisible \(a^2+b^2\)


Problem 2.4: Convergence in distribution to a constant
Davison (2003) Section 2.2, Exercise 2.
Let \(s_0\) be a constant. By writing \[
   \mathrm{P}(|S_n-s_0|\leq\varepsilon) =
   \mathrm{P}(S_n\leq s_0+\varepsilon) -
   \mathrm{P}(S_n\leq s_0-\varepsilon) ,
\] for \(\varepsilon > 0\), show that \(S_n\xrightarrow{D} s_0\) implies that \(S_n\xrightarrow{P} s_0\).






Tricking MathJax with invisible \(a^2+b^2\)


Problem 2.5: A truncated Poisson distribution
Davison (2003) Section 2.2, Exercise 8.
Truncated Poisson variables \(Y\) arise when counting quantities such as the sizes of groups, each of which must contain at least one element. The density is \[
\mathrm{P}(Y=y) = \frac{\theta^y\mathrm{e}^{-\theta}}{y!(1-e^{-\theta})} , \quad y = 1, 2, \dots, \quad \theta>0.
\]

Find an expression for \(\mathrm{E}\,(Y)=\mu(\theta)\) in terms of \(\theta\)

If \(Y_1,\dots,Y_n\) is a random sample for this density and \(n\to\infty\), give an argument for that \(\overline{Y}\xrightarrow{P} \mu(\theta)\). Hence deduce that \(\hat\theta = \mu^{-1}(\overline{Y})\xrightarrow{P}\theta\).



Finally, an interesting application:

Problem 2.6: A model for rare infections spreading in families
[see Davison, 4.9: Problem 12.]{smallgrey}
The following problem looks longer than the original in Davison, only because it is partitioned into steps and slightly simplified, and contains hints:
A family has two children \(A\) and \(B\). Child \(A\) catches an infectious disease \(D\) which is so rare that the probability that \(B\) catches it other than from \(A\) can be ignored.
Child \(A\) is infectious for a time \(U\) having probability density function
\[\begin{equation*}
    f_U(u) = \alpha \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha u},\  u \geq  0\text{, where }\alpha > 0.
\end{equation*}\]
To model spreading the infection to child \(B\) one assumes that in any small interval of time \([t, t + \delta t]\) in \([0, U)\), child \(B\) will catch the disease from \(A\) with probability \(\beta\cdot \delta t\), where \(\beta >0\).
Under these assumptions, the probability \(\rho\) that child \(B\) catches the infection from child \(A\) is given by \[\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho}
    \rho = \frac{\beta}{\gamma},\ \ \text{where\ }\gamma = \alpha +\beta.   \tag{1}
\end{equation}\]
In a family, where \(B\) actually is infected, the time \(T\) from infection of child \(A\) to infection of child \(B\) has an exponential distribution with density \[\begin{equation}\label{eq:gamma}
    f_T(t) = \gamma \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma t}.\tag{2}
\end{equation}\]
An epidemiologist observes \(n\) independent similar families, that is families with two children where at least one has been infected. In \(r\) of these families, the second child catches the disease from the first, at times \(t_1, \dots, t_r\)

Write down the likelihood of the data as the product of the probability of observing \(r\) and the likelihood of the fixed sample \(t_1, \dots , t_r\).
Find the maximum likelihood estimators \(\hat\rho\) and \(\hat\gamma\) of \(\rho\) and \(\gamma\), and the asymptotic variance of \(\hat\gamma\).
Find the maximum likelihood estimators for the original parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) from \(\hat\rho\) and \(\hat\gamma\).


 — (Fan Corner Mathematical Modelling) — 

For those of you, who are into mathematical modelling, you can solve the first to original sub problems from Davison: derive Equations \(\eqref{eq:rho}\) and \(\eqref{eq:gamma}\).
There are different ways to get to these results. You could solve the differential equation that is implied in the model, or follow the hints below:

To calculate the probability that B does catch the infection within the interval \([0,u)\), set \(\delta = u/m\) for \(m\in \mathbb{N}\). Then write the interval \([0,u)\) as union of \(m\) intervals of length \(\delta\). Let \(m\) go to infinity.
One way to find the distribution function of time \(T\) to infection for child B in the family where A and B have got the disease would again be to first calculate the probability that B does get infected in the interval \([0,t]\). You could separately consider cases where \(U<t\) and where \(U>t\), but perhaps you also have a smarter idea. For the final result, remember to divide by the probability that B gets infected, given A was infected.

title: Week 4: Exponential (Dispersion) Families and Introduction to GLM
text:
\(\renewcommand{\text}[1]{\textsf{#1}}\)
This week marks the transition to the second part of the course: generalized linear models (glm). Linear normal models describe the relation between a normal distributed variable \(Y\) and explanatory variables \(X_1, \dots, X_p\). Here we assume that the mean of \(Y\) is a linear combination of the explanatory variables. Generalized linear models extend this approach to variables \(Y\) with distribution that belongs to the class of so called exponential dispersion families. Also in other aspects, glms are more flexible than the ordinary linear normal model.
Exponential dispersion families include many known distributions, as different as the normal distribution and the Poisson distribution. We will discuss some common properties that are important for the construction of generalized linear models.

Exercises 4




Tricking MathJax with invisible \(a^2+b^2\)


Problem 4.1: Examples of exponential dispersion families (or not)


Consider the family of Gamma distributions with fixed shape parameter \(\alpha\) and with rate parameter \(\lambda\). The density is given as \[
     f(y) = \frac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}y^{\alpha-1} \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda y}.
\] Write this density in exponential dispersion family form, and identify the canonical parameter \(\theta\) as well as the function \(b\). Use these to show that the mean and variance of a Gamma\((\alpha, \lambda)\) distributed variable \(Y\) are \(\mathrm{E}\,Y = \alpha/\lambda\) and \(\mathrm{Var}\,Y = \alpha/\lambda^2\). Then determine the variance function and the canonical link function.
Give at least one example for a well known distribution family that is not an exponential dispersion family.







Tricking MathJax with invisible \(a^2+b^2\)


Problem 4.2: The inverse Gaussian distribution
(See Davison, Exercises 10.3.5. )
The inverse Gaussian distribution IG(\(\mu, \lambda\)) is important in the theory of stochastic processes. It has density \[
f(y;\mu, \lambda) = \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{2\pi y^3}} \exp\left(-\frac{\lambda(y-\mu)^2}{2\mu^2y}\right),\qquad y>0,\quad\lambda>0, \mu>0.
\]

Show that IG(\(\mu, \lambda\)) is exponential dispersion family. Give the canonical parameter \(\theta\), the dispersion parameter \(\phi\) and the functions \(b(\theta)\) and \(c(y;\phi)\) and show that its variance function is \(V(\mu)=\mu^3\).
Explain the role of the Inverse Gaussian distribution in stochastic processes (Brownian motion) - you can use the Wikipedia page as a (first) source. If you like, illustrate with a simulation.







Tricking MathJax with invisible \(a^2+b^2\)


Problem 4.3: The binomial distribution converges to a Poisson distribution
Davison, Section 2.6 Problem 3:
Show that a binomial random variable \(R\) with size parameter \(m\) and probability \(\pi\) has cumulant-generating function \[K(t)=m\log(1-\pi+\pi\mathrm{e}^t).\]
Find \(\lim K(t)\) as \(m\to\infty\) and \(\pi\to 0\) in such a way that \(m\pi \to \lambda>0\). Show that \[
\mathrm{P}(R=r) \to \frac{\lambda^r}{r!}\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda},
\] and hence establish that \(R\) converges in distribution to a Poisson random variable. This yields the Poisson approximation to the binomial distribution, sometimes called the law of small numbers.
For a numerical check in the R language, try

y <- 0:10
lambda <- 1
m <- 10
p <- lambda/m
round(cbind(y = y, 
            binomial = pbinom(y, size = m, prob = p), 
            Poisson = ppois(y, lambda)), digits = 3)

with various other values of \(m\) and \(\lambda\).
A little extra: for a visualization of the approximation, you can also make a joint graph of both distribution functions. Try also here to change \(m\) and/or \(\lambda\).

lambda <- 10

m <- 20
p <- lambda/m

ymax <- as.integer(round(2*lambda + 1)) # a good range of y-values
yvalues <- 0:ymax
# function stepfun needs 1 more value for the y-axis (here F(y)) than for the x-axis
binfoo <- stepfun(yvalues[-(ymax + 1)], pbinom(yvalues, size = m, prob = p))
poisfoo <- stepfun(yvalues[-(ymax + 1)], ppois(yvalues, lambda))

plot(binfoo, 
    main = "binomial and Poisson distribution function",
    xlab = "y", ylab = "F(y)")
plot(poisfoo, add = TRUE, col = 2)














Tricking MathJax with invisible \(a^2+b^2\)


Problem 4.4: The Weibull distribution for life times
Davison, Section 2.6, Problem 7, minus a typo, plus a bit more explanation, a simulation, and an extra question (c):
A random variable \(Y\) with the Weibull distribution with shape parameter \(\kappa\) and scale parameter \(\lambda\) has distribution function \[
F_Y(y;\kappa,\lambda)= 1-\exp(-(y/\lambda)^\kappa), \quad x>0, \ \ \lambda,\,\kappa > 0.
\] The idea that a system with many similar components will fail when the weakest component fails has led to widespread use of this distribution in industrial reliability. Part a) illustrates this.

Suppose that \(X_1,\dots, X_m\) are independent identically distributed continuous nonnegative random variables such that as \(x\to 0\), the density and distribution functions are asymptotically \(f(x)=a x^{\kappa-1}\) and \(F(x)=a/\kappa \,x^\kappa\), where \(a,\kappa > 0\).
Let \(Y=\min(X_1,\dots, X_m)\) and let \(W=(a/\kappa)^{1/\kappa}m^{1/\kappa}Y\). Show that as \(m\to\infty\), \(W\) has as its limiting distribution the Weibull distribution with shape \(\kappa\) and scale \(\lambda=1\).


Hint, background, demonstration
Hint: a very useful formula in many situations of life is \[
      \lim_{n\to\infty} (1+x/n)^n = \mathrm{e}^x.
    \]
Background and demonstration In certain application areas, life times of small components are thought to behave like the random variables \(X\) mentioned above. Here is a simulation experiment where \(X\) has distribution given by \(f(x)= a x^{\kappa-1}\) for \(0\leq x \leq (\kappa/a)^{1/\kappa}\). Play with the values \(a\), \(\kappa\) and \(m\).











Explain why a probability plot for the Weibull distribution may be based on plotting the logarithm of the \(r\)th order statistic against \(\log(-\log(1-\frac{r}{n+1}))\), and give the slope and intercept of such a plot.
Use this idea to check graphically whether the data in Table 1.2 follow Weibull distributions.


Hints and remarks
The \(r\)-th order statistic is the \(r\)-th smallest value in a sample \(Y_1, ..., Y_n\). It is denoted as \(Y_{[r]}\).
The plot that Davison suggests is a variant of the qq-plot.  In a usual qq-plot,the \(x\)- values of the plotted points are \(F^{-1}(1/(n+1)), F^{-1}(2/(n+1)), \dots, F^{-1}(n/(n+1))\), and the \(y\)- values are \(y_{[1]}, y_{[2]}\dots, y_{[n]}\). If \(F\) is the distribution that generated the sample, the points should lie approximately on an identity line with slope 1 and intercept 0.
A normal qq-plot compares the order statistics against the quantiles of a standard normal distribution. If the data come from a \(N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) distribution with \(\mu \neq 0\) and/or \(\sigma^2\neq 1\), the points would still lie approximately on a straight line, but with intercept \(\mu\) and slope \(\sigma\). Try for example








Table 1.2 can be found in Davison, on p.4. The data are contained as dataframe springs in R package SMPracticals that you installed a while ago :-). The dataset contains a variable cens that indicates if the actual life time has been within the experiment: if cens == 0, the life time was longer and has been censored (by the length of experiment). In all cases where stress was 800 Nm or higher, the true life times have been measured.
You can try out the suggested plot with simulated values from the Weibull distribution:











The family of Weibull distributions with parameters \(\kappa>0\) and \(\lambda>0\) is not (an) exponential family. Why? What, if we restrict to a given \(\kappa>0\)? Is it exponential family then? Is it exponential dispersion family?

title: Week 6: Algorithms, and models for count data
text:
\(\renewcommand{\text}[1]{\textsf{#1}}\)
We will conclude the general topics about mle for now with a look at the actual algorithms behind maximum likelihood estimation as done by function glm: Fisher scoring and iteratively reweighted least squares.
Then we continue with particular generalized linear models, for binary and count data. For binary or binomial data (proportions of successes in Bernoulli trials), numerous link functions have been suggested. They can be motivated by a “model hidden behind the model”: we imagine that the success of a Bernoulli trial depends on an unknown “latent” variable. An important application for the binomial model are contingency tables. The straightforward choice for count data are Poisson distributions. We will see that the canonical link function (log link) has a direct interpretation as “multiplicative” model.
If there is time, we will look at the theory behind the AIC criterion for model fit.

Problem 6.1: LD\(_{50}\) for the “bliss” data – compare different link functions.
Dataset bliss from the SMpracticals library contains data on mortality of flour-beetles as a function of dose of the poison carbon disulphide (Bliss, 1935, Table IV). To analyze these data, Bliss used a binomial generalized linear model with probit link.

Problem 6.2: Model parsimonity: a simulation experiment.
(Adapted from Agresti (2015), exercises 4.36 and 4.37)
For \(x\) between 0 and 100, suppose the normal linear model holds with \[\mathrm{E}\,(y) = 45 + 0.1x + 5\cdot 10^{-4}\, x^2 + 5\cdot 10^{-7}\, x^3 + 5\cdot 10^{-10}\,x^4 +5\cdot 10^{-13} \,x^5\]
and \(\sigma = 10.0\). Randomly generate \(n=25\) observations from the model, with \(x\) having a uniform distribution between 0 and 100. Fit the simple model \[
M_1:\quad \mu_j= \beta_0 + \beta_1x_j,
\] an “intermediate” model \[
M_2:\quad \mathrm{E}\,(y) = \beta_0+\beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2,
\] and the “correct” model \[
M_5:\quad \mathrm{E}\,(y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \cdots + \beta_5x^5.
\]
Construct plots, showing the data, the true relationship, and the model fits. For each model, summarize the quality of the fit by the average of \(|\hat\mu_j - \mu_j|\), that is, \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n |\hat\mu_j - \mu_j|\), where \(\mu_j=\mathrm{E}\,(y_j)\) and \(\hat\mu_j\) is the \(j\)th fitted value, depending on the model: for example in model \(M_1\), \(\mu_j=\beta_0+\beta_1 x_j\) and \(\hat\mu_j=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1 x_j\).
Repeat the experiment several times with different \(x\)-values. It is also interesting to look what happens if you increase the number of observations substantially, or change the true coefficients.
Summarize, and explain what this exercise illustrates about model parsimony. What does the fit of the “correct” model \(M_5\) illustrate about (multi)collinearity?

Hint
To fit polynomial models such as \(M_2\) in R, you can directly specify the components: y ~ I(x) + I(x^2) or use the convenient function poly, namely y ~ poly(x, 2, raw = TRUE).

(From Agresti, 7.28)
Other than a formal goodness-of-fit test, one analysis that provides a sense of whether a particular GLM is plausible is the following:
Suppose the ML fitted equation were the true equation. At the observed \(x\)-values for the \(n\) observations, randomly generate \(n\) variates with distributions specified by the fitted GLM. Construct scatterplots. Do they look like the scatterplots that were actually observed?
Do this for a Poisson loglinear model for the horseshoe crab data1, with \(y\) = number of satellites and \(x\) = width. Problem 6.4: Modelling variance in repeated experiments.
Davison, Problem 10.10.8, plus hints.

Show that the scaled chi-squared density with known degrees of freedom \(\nu\), \[
f(y;\sigma, \nu)=\frac{y^{\nu/2-1}}{2^{\nu/2}\sigma^\nu\Gamma(\nu/2)}\exp\left(-\frac{y}{2\sigma^2}\right),\quad y>0, \sigma>0,\nu=1,2,\dots,
\] is exponential dispersion family. Express the canonical parameter \(\theta\) and the dispersion parameter \(\phi\) as functions of \(\nu\) and \(\sigma^2\).
Hence derive an expression for its \(r\) th cumulant, \(r\geq 1\).

Hint

Consider \(\nu\) as a known constant. Several choices for \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) are possible, and \(\phi\) is a constant, too. One possible choice is \(\phi = -2\); with this choice, the canonical link function depends on \(\nu\). Another option is \(\phi = -2/\nu\) — check it out :-) If you need a reminder for the moment generating function look at the top of Davison, page 481. Then you easily recall the cumulant generating function.

The yield of an industrial process was measured \(r_i\) times independently at m different temperatures \(t_i\) . The resulting yields \(Z_{ij} , i = 1,\dots ,m, j = 1, \dots , r_i\) may be assumed to be independent and normally distributed with both \(\zeta_i\) and variances \(\tau_i\) dependent on \(t_i\).
Explain how the sums of squares \(Y_i =\sum_{j=1}^{r_i}(Z_{ij}-\overline{Z}_i)^2\), where \(\overline{Z}_i=\frac{1}{r_i}\sum_{j=1}^ {r_i} Z_{ij},\) may be used to assess the dependence of variance on temperature in a suitable generalized linear model.

Problem 6.5: Deviance for the binary logistic model.

This exercise deals with data \(y_1,\dots,y_n\) that come frome independent Bernoulli experiments with probability parameter \(\pi_1,\dots, \pi_n\).
A little extra before solving parts a-c: identify the distribution of \(Y_j\) with \(\mathrm{P}(Y_j=1) = \pi_j\) and \(\mathrm{P}(Y_j=0) = 1-\pi_j\) as an exponential dispersion distribution with dispersion parameter \(\phi=1\). Determine the canonical parameter \(\theta\) and the function \(b\).
Here is the exercise text from Davison:
Data \(y_1,\dots, y_n\) are assumed to follow a binary logistic model in which \(y_j\) takes value 1 with probability \(\pi_j = \exp(x^{\mathsf{T}}_j\beta)/(1 + \exp(x^{\mathsf{T}}_j\beta))\) and value 0 otherwise, for \(j = 1, \dots , n\).

\] and that the likelihood equation is \(X^{\mathsf{T}}y = X^{\mathsf{T}}\hat\pi\). Hence show that the deviance is a function of the \(\hat\pi_j\) alone.

D = -2n \left(\bar{y} \log \bar{y} + (1-\bar{y}) \log(1 - \bar{y})\right).
\] Comment on the implications for using \(D\) to measure the discrepancy between the data and fitted model.
Assuming that \(\pi_1=\dots=\pi_n = \pi\) (as in part (b)), show that Pearson’s statistic, formula (10.21) in Davison, \[
   P = \frac{1}{\phi}\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{(y_j-\hat\mu_j)^2}{V(\hat\mu_j)/a_j},
\]
is identically equal to \(n\). Comment.

\(\renewcommand{\text}[1]{\textsf{#1}}\)
This week, will start with the third big topic: Bayesian statistics.
Lectures and exercises will be mainly based on the book BJ Reich, SK Ghosh (2019): Bayesian Statistical Methods.
The book starts with a review of probability background (Section 1.1) and of the Bayes rule for calculating conditional probabilities / conditional densities (Section 1.2). You can use these introductory sections for reference :-)
I will very briefly recall the Bayes rule in the first lecture on Wednesday. Then, I will introduce the basic ideas of Bayesian statistics.
On Friday, we will learn about conjugate priors: prior distributions that match well with the likelihood, such that the form of the posterior is analytically known. Then we will look at the distinction of informative and uninformative priors, and “improper” priors.

The researcher gathers a sample of \(n\) trees from the forest and \(X_2\) belong to the species of interest. The model for the data is \(X_2\mid X_1 \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n, \lambda X_1)\) where \(\lambda\in [0, 1]\) is the probability of detecting the species given it is present.

\(\mathrm{P}(X_1 = 0)\).
\(\mathrm{P}(X_2 = 0)\).
\(\mathrm{P}(X_1 = 0 \mid X_2 = 0)\).

\(\mathrm{P}(X_1 = 0 \mid X_2 = 1)\).

The denominator in the formula for the posterior distribution (1.36 in Ghosh) is then a sum.

This week’s only lecture concentrates on the Gibbs sampler, a method that allows to generate random samples from the posterior distribution a multidimensional parameter. In essence it consists in updating one element of the multidimensional parameter at a time.
The other very important MCMC method is the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, that enables us to simulate from a distribution that is known up to a constant. If time allows, we will start with the Metropolis algorithm in the end of Friday’s lecture.
In order to understand the algorithms, you will implement them yourselves in R. Later in this course you will use software “off the shelf” to run MCMC. You will learn to use JAGS and the R package rjags to analyze simple Bayesian models.

Data Workshop on Wednesday

Data: An Agricultural Experiment About Ants
A researcher interested in ants and their benefit for agriculture in the Midwest, Karl A. Roeder, has posted a dataset on USDA, https://doi.org/10.15482/USDA.ADC/28454771.
The data set contains two .csv files: Metadata and Master Data, you can download them as Ant_Experiment.csv and Metadata for Ant Tillage Experiment.csv from the Google Drive.
The Metadata describes column variables for the Master Data file that contains all of the information used in the analyses. This project encompasses two years of work (12 weeks per year) where ants were sampled along 8 transects of corn with tillage, 8 transects of corn without tillage, 8 transects of soybeans with tillage, and 8 transects of soybeans without tillage. Sentinel prey stations were deployed for 48hrs after ant sampling and contained ~60 corn earworm eggs to provide a quantitative assessment of pest predation by beneficial ants.

Tentative methods from the paper  (= background information from authors)

Study Site
Research was conducted at the Eastern South Dakota Soil and Water Research Farm in Brookings, South Dakota, USA (44.352882, -96.803453). Historically, multiple crops have been grown at this location including corn (Zea mays) and soybean (Glycine max) with and without tillage (hereafter referred to as Till and No-Till). In 2015, four ~0.4ha blocks were setup in a complete block design that each included four 50m x 20m equal sized plots of till corn, no-till corn, till soybean, and no-till soybean. The crops in each of these plots were rotated yearly with the other crop (corn to soybean and soybean to corn), but the tillage treatment of spring disking was kept in place such that the same plots were always tilled or not tilled.


Ant activity: abundance and species richness
Ants were sampled weekly in all plots from June to August in both 2021 and 2022. We setup two equidistant transects within each plot (N=32 transects per week) that were spaced at least 20m apart. Within each transect, we evenly placed on the ground twenty 1.5ml conical microcentrifuge tubes (Midland Scientific, USA) that contained a cotton ball that was saturated with a 20% sucrose solution. This baiting technique is common for ant studies measuring activity and has been used in numerous studies across a variety of ecosystems. For all sample weeks, tubes were deployed at 0800, collected after one hour, and returned to the lab for processing (i.e. counting the number of ants and species) and data analysis. The morning sampling time was chosen based on pilot trials in 2020 that indicated ants would not forage earlier do to potentially cold temperatures in the morning (e.g. <10°C) or during the middle of the day when temperatures were too hot (e.g. >50°C). These limiting abiotic conditions were exacerbated in June when vegetation was sparse.
Environmental variables (air, ground, and soil temperatures along with relative humidity) were measured in between bait tube deployment/pickup at the beginning, middle, and end of each transect during each sampling event. Air temperature and relative humidity were measured using a Kestrel 3000 weather station (Kestrel Instruments, USA), ground temperature was measured using a Fluke 62 max IR thermometer (Fluke Corporation, USA), and soil temperature was measured using a Weber instant-read digital meat thermometer (Weber, USA). Values from each variable were then averaged per transect for further analysis.


Measuring pest predation using sentinel prey
We measured predation of pest insects as one ecosystem service provided by ants during each sampling period (N=24 total weeks) by placing one sentinel prey station in the crop row directly north of each transect immediately after bait tubes were collected. Each sentinel prey station was comprised of ~60 freeze-killed corn earworm eggs (Helicoverpa zea; Frontier Agricultural Sciences, USA) that were glued to a small piece of a flash card and then placed in a small petri dish within a vertebrate exclosure. Corn earworm eggs have regularly been used as sentinel prey for ants in agricultural studies due to their relevance as a crop pest. After 48hrs in the field, sentinel prey were collected and the remaining eggs were counted to quantify the proportion of pest insects that had been attacked.

title: Mixed priors: Example from Figure 2.5, R&G
text:
Figure 2.5 in Reich & Ghosh shows prior and posterior distributions in a Beta-binomial model, for two different priors and a mixture of both priors.1
Here is one possibility how you can generate a similar figure in base R.
The first code chunk implements numeric integration to get the posterior. Lazy, lazy! In this example, we know the analytical solution and could have implemented it.
# making a vector of x-values (theta) by hand
deltatheta <- 0.0002
theta <- seq(0, 1, deltatheta)

# the two priors, taken in the values of thetavector
prior1 <- dbeta(theta, 2000, 2000)
prior2 <- dbeta(theta, 1, 1)

mixprior <- .5*(prior1 + prior2)

# the binomial model, also a vector
likelihood <- dbinom(963, 1800, theta)

# calculating posterior: divide by integral to normalize
# here we approximate the integral by a (Riemann) sum
get_posterior <- function(likelihood, prior, dt = deltatheta){
  unnormalized_posterior <- likelihood * prior
  integral <- sum(unnormalized_posterior) * dt
  unnormalized_posterior / integral
}

# the single posteriors, and the posterior of the mixture
post1 <- get_posterior(likelihood, prior1)
post2 <- get_posterior(likelihood, prior2)

mixpost <- get_posterior(likelihood, mixprior, deltatheta)
Here are the plots, made to look alike Figure 2.5 in R&G
Code
plot(theta, prior1, type="l", col = "purple", lwd = 1,
     xlim = c(.4, .6), ylim = range(c(post1, post2, prior1, prior2)),
     xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "Density")
lines(theta, post1, col = "purple", lwd = 2)

lines(theta, prior2, col = "forestgreen", lwd = 1, lty = "dashed")
lines(theta, post2, col = "forestgreen", lwd = 2, lty = "dashed")

section: Markov chains in discrete time with finite or countable state space
text:
Markov chains in discrete time with finite or countable state space




Tricking MathJax with invisible \(a^2+b^2\)

In the introductory probability course (“ISS”), you learned about Markov chains \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) with a finite or countable state space, that is, the \(X_i\) take only values from a finite or countable set \(S\) of outcomes. Markov chains have the Markov property that says that the conditional probability of \(X_{n+1}\) taking a value \(x\in S\), given that \(X_n=x_n\), does not depend on the previous values of \(X_{n-1}, X_{n-2},\dots\), see for example Pishro-Nik, Section 11.2: \[
\mathrm{P}(X_{n+1} = x\mid X_n=x_n, X_{n-1}=x_{n-1}, \dots) =
\mathrm{P}(X_{n+1} = x\mid X_n=x_n)
\]
A Markov chain with finite or countable state space is called homogeneous, if its transition probabilities do not depend on the index \(n\): \[
   p_{ij} = \mathrm{Prob}(X_{n+1} = j\mid X_n=i) .
\] To stretch that the homogeneity refers to shifting the index \(n\), which is seen as “time”, one also calls such Markov chains time-homogeneous.
Sometimes, the starting value of the chain is denoted by \(X_0\), in particular, when one wants to emphasize that this value is arbitrarily chosen by the user.

Stationary and limiting distribution of a homogeneous Markov chain with finite state space
The distribution of the chain at “time” \(n\), that is, the distribution of \(X_n\), depends on the distribution of \(X_{n-1}\) and thus indirectly on the distribution of \(X_{n-2}\) etc. If it holds for a distribution \(\pi\), that \[X_{n} \sim \pi \implies X_{n+1}\sim \pi,\] then we call that distribution a stationary distribution of the Markov chain.
For a Markov chain with finite state space that is irreducible, one can show that the stationary distribution is the limiting distribution, that is, no matter what the value or distribution of \(X_1\) is, the distribution of the chain converges to \(\pi\): \[
  \mathrm{P}(X_n\in A)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\pi(A)\quad \text{for all } A\subseteq S
\] that is, \[
  X_n\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{D} X,\quad\text{where } X\sim \pi.
\]
see Pishro-Nik, Section 11.2.6
The concept of Markov chains as discussed above can be generalized in two ways: to continuous time chains, where we index the \(X\)es with a continuous variable \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), or to continuous state space, such as \(S\subset \mathbb{R}\) (or both).

title: Markov chains
section: Markov chains with continuous state space
text:
Markov chains with continuous state space
In the context of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, we most often need continuous state spaces, but stick to discrete time, that is indexing with integers.
For many random variables on \(\mathbb{R}\), the probability of taking a given value \(x\) is zero. E.g., when \(X\sim N(0,1)\), we can safely say the \(\mathrm{Prob}(X = 0.2) = 0\). But for the same random variable, the probability of falling into the interval \([0,0.2]\) is larger than zero. Instead of looking at the probability that \(X_{n+1}=x\), we look at the probability \(X_{n+1}\in A\) to define the Markov property for chains with continuous state space: \[
\mathrm{P}(X_{n+1} \in A \mid X_n\in A_n, X_{n-1}\in A_{n-1}, \dots) =
\mathrm{P}(X_{n+1} \in A\mid X_n\in A_n),
\] where \(A, A_n,A_{n-1},\dots\subseteq S\) are any sets that make sense in this context (for those who have had a course on measure theory, they are “measureable sets”).


Transition (kernel) densities of homogeneous Markov chains
Transition probabilities as for Markov chains with countable state space are now replaced by transition kernel densities. A kernel density \(k\) is a nonnegative function on \(S\times S\), and for each \(x\in S\), \(k(., x)\) is a probability density on \(S\) that depends on \(x\). In a time-homogeneous Markov chain, the transition kernel \(k\) is the same for all times \(n\). Then \[
\mathrm{Prob}(X_{n+1} \in A\mid X_n\in B) = \int_B \int_A k(y, x) \mathrm{d}y \, P_n(\mathrm{d}x),
\] and \(k(., x)\) is the probability density of \(X_{n+1}\) when \(X_n=x\), for any \(n\). The inner integral, \(\int_A k(y, x) \mathrm{d}y\), can be interpreted as the conditional probability that \(X_{n+1}\in A\) given that \(X_n = x\). That integral can only take values between 0 and 1.


Stationary and limiting distribution
The definition of stationary distribution carries right over from the case of Markov chains with finite or countable state space. Now, let \(\pi\) be the stationary distribution of a Markov chain with transition density \(k\), and assume that \(X_n\sim \pi\). Then for all \(y\in S\), \[
\pi(y) = \int_S k(y, x)\pi(x) \mathrm{d} x.
\] This can be proven quite quickly using tools from measure theory, but more importantly, it has an intuitive explanation 🙂

For Markov chains with general state space (including continuous state space) \(S\), we have a theorem that ensures that

A homogeneous Markov chain \(X_1, X_2,\dots\), that has stationary distribution \(\pi\), and is irreducible, aperiodic and Harris recurrent, always has \(\pi\) as its limiting distribution. That is, the chain converges in distribution to \(\pi\) irrespective of the starting value \(X_0=x_0\), \[
\mathrm{P}(X_n\in A \mid X_0=x_0) \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}{} \pi(A),\quad\text{for all }x_0\in S.
\]

The technical conditions of this theorem are usually fulfilled in MCMC applications. We will later deal with methods to check if this convergence holds, and to judge how fast the convergence is, see Reich & Ghosh, Section 3.4.

title: Crossvalidating a Bayesian model
text:
Often, we have data with covariates that do not really contribute to the explanation. Consider the following situation:

We have count data \(y_i\) that supposedly come from a Poisson model, where the parameter depends on a covariate \(x_i\) in that the linear predictor is a polynomium of \(x_i\). We want to find the polynomium that best fits the data, but don’t know the degree og the polynomium.

Assuming a canonical (log) link, the model formally reads: \[
  Y_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_i),\quad\mu_i=\mathbb{E}Y_i = \exp(\eta_i),\quad\eta_i=\beta_1 +\beta_2x_i +\beta_3 x_i^2+\dots+\beta_p x_i^{p-1}.
\] The code below simulates a example with quadratic polynomial, so \(p=3\), where I chose \(\boldsymbol{\beta}=(1, 0.1, 0.03)\), \(n=51\) and \(\boldsymbol{x} = 0, 0.2, \dots, 10\):

set.seed(123) # make it reproducible

x <- seq(0, 10, 0.2) # 51 values
# model matrix
X <- cbind(1, x, x^2)
beta <- c(1, 0.1, 0.03)

# eta <-  beta[1] + beta[2]*x + beta[3]*x^2 
# in matrix form:
eta <- X %*% beta
# log link, i.e. inverse is exponential
mu <- exp(eta)

Y <- rpois(length(mu), mu)

Visualize the data, together with \(\mu\):

par(mfrow = c(1,2))
plot(x, Y)
lines(x, mu)
# plot log(Y) and log(mu) against x to show the form of function eta(x)
plot(x, log(Y))
lines(x, log(mu))








Now I want to analyze the data in a Bayesian way and look at the predicted \(\hat{Y}_i\). In order to find out the degree of the polynomial, I will apply models with different degree, that is, varying \(p\). To this end, I wrap the whole analysis into a function. This function takes the data, and a vector of \(x\)-values where we want to make the prediction. Thus, we can use the function later for cross validation.

library(rjags)

Loading required package: coda


Linked to JAGS 4.3.1


Loaded modules: basemod,bugs

PoissonPolynomial_predict <- function(Y, x, x_pred = x, p=3, 
                              truebeta = beta, # for initialization
                              quiet = TRUE){
  model_string <-"model{
    # Likelihood
    for (i in 1:n){
      Y[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])
      log(mu[i]) <- inprod(X[i, ], beta[])
    }
    # Priors
    for (j in 1:p) {beta[j] ~ dnorm(0, .01)}
    # Y hat values: posterior means for prediction matrix
    for (i in 1:n_pred){
      Yhat[i] <- exp(inprod(X_pred[i, ], beta[]))
    }
  }"
  
  # make matrix of x^0, x^2, ..., x^{p-1}
  X <- t(sapply(x, function(z) z^(1:p -1)))
  X_pred <- t(sapply(x_pred, function(z) z^(1:p -1)))
  
  if (p <= length(truebeta)) beta_init <- truebeta[1:p]
  if (p > length(truebeta)) beta_init <- c(truebeta, rep(0, p - length(truebeta)))
  
  model <- jags.model(textConnection(model_string),
                      data = list(Y = Y, X = X, X_pred =X_pred,
                                  p = p, n = length(Y), 
                                  n_pred = length(x_pred)), 
                      inits = list(beta = beta_init), 
                      n.chains = 1,
                      quiet = quiet)
  # burn in - should not be necessary since we cheat by starting with true values
  update(model, 1000, progress.bar = "none")
  
  # want to know the predicted lambda = Yhat
  samples <- coda.samples(model,
                          variable.names = c("Yhat"),
                          n.iter = 5000,
                          progress.bar = "none")
  # get posterior values
  mu_post <- samples[[1]] # a S x n matrix
  # return posterior mean
  apply(mu_post, 2, mean)
}

The next function is for conveniently printing goodness-of-fit statistics, MSE, MAD and LS. I exluded BIAS, because it does not give much information in our case.

goodfits <- function(Yobs, mu_hat){
   Y_hat = mu_hat # easy here: just another name
   c(
    MSE = sum((Y_hat - Yobs)^2),
  #  BIAS = sum(Y_hat - Yobs), gives not much information in this case: dropped it
    MAD = sum(abs(Y_hat - Yobs)),
    LS = sum(dpois(Yobs, mu_hat, log = TRUE))
  )  
}

Yhat5 <- PoissonPolynomial_predict(Y, x, p=5)

For all criteria, we can see a big difference between a merely linear model (\(p=2\)) and the quadratic model (\(p=3\)), but increasing the degree of the polynomium further does not give big changes anymore.
Here, we have used the same data for Bayesian model fitting and for assessing the goodness of fit. This is not good practice (why?), therefore we try crossvalidation instead.

# ================ Cross validation "by hand" ===================

# select K groups of roughly same size

make_groups <- function(n, K = n, random = TRUE){
  # group size n_i : a vector of K elements
  # first K mod n groups are a bit larger
  
  nrep <- (n-1) %/% K + 1 
  # number of necessary replications. E.g. if K=3, and n=8, need 3 replications
  
  g_i <- as.factor(rep(1:K, nrep)[1:n])
  
  # check it with table(g_i)
  
  # if random, shuffle group allocation of individuals, 
  #   and return the shuffled values
  # otherwise just return g_i
  if (random) sample(g_i) else g_i
}
# a function for crossvalidation in our polynomial Poisson example
crossvalidate <- function(Y, x, p = 3, K = length(Y), randomgroups = TRUE){
  stopifnot(K > 1) # only a check if there is a wrong input value
  
  n <- length(Y)
  groups <- make_groups(n, K, randomgroups) 
  Yhat <- numeric(n)
  for (k in 1: K){
    testset <- groups == k
    training <- !testset
    Yhat[testset] <- PoissonPolynomial_predict(Y[training], x[training],
                                               x[testset], p=p)
  }
  Yhat
}

Yha4 <- crossvalidate(Y, x, K=5, p = 4)
Yha5 <- crossvalidate(Y, x, K=5, p = 5)

title: Gibbs sampler for bivariate normal distribution
text:
In the bivariate normal example (Reich & Ghosh, p. 81), we want to simulate realizations \(\boldsymbol{\theta}=(U,V)\) from a normal distribution with zero mean and variance 1 for the components, and correlation \(\rho\) between the parameters. That is, \[
\pmatrix{U\\V} \sim \mathrm{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}), \quad\boldsymbol{\mu}=\pmatrix{0\\0},\ \ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\pmatrix{1&\rho\\ \rho & 1}.
\] The standard library MASS has a convenient function mvrnorm to simulate from a \(d\)-variate normal. It returns a matrix with \(d\) column vectors.












Now we do this by hand, with a Gibbs sampler.
The conditional distribution \(X_2\mid X_1\) of a random vector \(\boldsymbol{X}\) with bivariate normal distribution, \[\pmatrix{X_1\\X_2} \sim \mathrm{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}),\quad \boldsymbol{\mu}=(\mu_1,\mu_2)^{\mathsf{T}},\quad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\pmatrix{\sigma_1^2&\sigma_1\sigma_2\rho\\ \sigma_1\sigma_2\rho & \sigma_2^2}\] is given by \[
  X_2\mid X_1=x_1\ \  \sim \ \ \mathrm{N}(\mu_2 + \rho\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}(x_1-\mu_1), (1-\rho^2)\sigma_2^2)
\] see R&G, page 14.
This gives us the full conditionals in the model for \(\boldsymbol{\theta}=(U,V)^\mathsf{T}\) with \(\boldsymbol{\mu}=(0,0)^\mathsf{T},\ \ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\pmatrix{1&\rho\\ \rho & 1}\), that is, \(\mu_1=\mu_2=0, \sigma_1=\sigma_2=1\), as \[
  U | V=v\ \sim\  \mathrm{N}(\rho\cdot v, 1-\rho^2)\quad \text{ and }\quad V | U=u\ \sim\  \mathrm{N}(\rho\cdot u, 1-\rho^2).
\]
Now we can set up a Gibbs sampler. Since the support of the bivariate normal distribution is the whole \(\mathbb{R}^2\), we expect the sampler to converge to the distribution no matter where we start.












The simulated point clouds look very similar to the ones we obtained with mvrnorm.
Compare trace plots of one component, say, \(U\):






🤔 Can you see a difference? Does the choice of \(\rho\) have any influence?

title: Metropolis-Hastings Markov Chain Exercise
text:
Simulate from a distribution with density proportional to \(h\), \[
h(x) = \begin{cases}
x^5 \sin(x), & 0 < x < \pi\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}.
\] Use the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm with proposal density
\[
q(y, x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\exp\left(-\frac{(y-x)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).
\] 🤔? How can you simulate the proposals?
The resulting algorithm is called a “random walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm”, because it adds random increments to the current value.
It is a symmetric proposal, i.e. . Therefore the Metropolis-Hastings-Green ratio is simplified:
\[
r(x, y) = \frac{h(y)q(x, y)}{h(x)q(y, x)}=\frac{h(y)}{h(x)}.
\] 🤔? Don’t we risk to run into problems by proposing a new value outside the support?

Davison, Example 10.21, discusses a moderately simple model to explain soccer outcomes.

title: Binary Data: Analysis, Modelling
text:
Background idea
It is natural in many cases to assume that the Bernoulli outcome \(Y_j\) is determined by a latent random variable \(Z_j\).
The outcome \(Y_j\) is positive if and only if \(Z_j\) exceeds a critical threshold, which can be defined to be zero (\(0\)). Thus,
\[
  Y_j = \begin{cases}
  1,& Z_j > 0\\
  0,& Z_j \leq 0
  \end{cases}.
\]
The variable \(Z_j\) itself depends linearly on the covariate vector \(\mathbf{x}_j\), and a random offset \(\varepsilon_j\sim F\), \[
Z_j=\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\gamma} +\varepsilon_j\cdot\sigma
\]
\(F\) is the tolerance distribution.

title: Binary Data: Analysis, Modelling
section: Link function in the latent variable model
text:
Link function in the latent variable model
Mean of \(Y\) is \(\mathrm{E}\,Y=\pi\).
Let \(F\) be the tolerance distribution, i.e. the distribution of \(\varepsilon\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi &= \mathrm{P}(Y=1) = \mathrm{P}(Z>0)\\
&=\mathrm{P}(\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\gamma} + \varepsilon\sigma > 0)\\
&=\mathrm{P}(\varepsilon > - \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\gamma} / \sigma)\qquad (\text{write }
\boldsymbol{\beta}:=\boldsymbol{\gamma} / \sigma)\\
&=1 - F( - \underbrace{\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\eta})
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus, the link function corresponding to tolerance distribution \(F\) is found by inverting \(\pi = 1-F(-\eta)\),  namely
\[
g(\pi) = \eta = -F^{-1}(1-\pi)
\]

shortcut: symmetric tolerance distribution
If \(F\) is symmetric around \(0\) then \[
\pi  =1 - F( - \eta) = F(\eta)
\]
thus the link function is \[
  g(\pi) = F^{-1}(\pi)
\]

title: Binary Data: Analysis, Modelling
text:
Background idea
It is natural in many cases to assume that the Bernoulli outcome \(Y_j\) is determined by a latent random variable \(Z_j\).
The outcome \(Y_j\) is positive if and only if \(Z_j\) exceeds a critical threshold, which can be defined to be zero (\(0\)). Thus,
\[
  Y_j = \begin{cases}
  1,& Z_j > 0\\
  0,& Z_j \leq 0
  \end{cases}.
\]
The variable \(Z_j\) itself depends linearly on the covariate vector \(\mathbf{x}_j\), and a random offset \(\varepsilon_j\sim F\), \[
Z_j=\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\gamma} +\varepsilon_j\cdot\sigma
\]
\(F\) is the tolerance distribution.

title: Binary Data: Analysis, Modelling
section: Link function in the latent variable model
text:
Link function in the latent variable model
Mean of \(Y\) is \(\mathrm{E}\,Y=\pi\).
Let \(F\) be the tolerance distribution, i.e. the distribution of \(\varepsilon\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi &= \mathrm{P}(Y=1) = \mathrm{P}(Z>0)\\
&=\mathrm{P}(\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\gamma} + \varepsilon\sigma > 0)\\
&=\mathrm{P}(\varepsilon > - \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\gamma} / \sigma)\qquad (\text{write }
\boldsymbol{\beta}:=\boldsymbol{\gamma} / \sigma)\\
&=1 - F( - \underbrace{\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\eta})
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus, the link function corresponding to tolerance distribution \(F\) is found by inverting \(\pi = 1-F(-\eta)\),  namely
\[
g(\pi) = \eta = -F^{-1}(1-\pi)
\]


shortcut: symmetric tolerance distribution
If \(F\) is symmetric around \(0\) then \[
\pi  =1 - F( - \eta) = F(\eta)
\]
thus the link function is \[
  g(\pi) = F^{-1}(\pi)
\]

title: The truth about the negative binomial distribution and glm.nb
section: Is the negative binomial model an exponential dispersion family?
text:
Is the negative binomial model an exponential dispersion family?
Well, it depends.
Let us look at the probability density function. We had introduced the negative binomial distribution as the distribution of a Poisson variable with parameter \(\lambda\) drawn randomly from a Gamma distribution with shape \(k\) and scale \(\mu/k\).
The probability density then takes the form \[
\begin{aligned}
  f(y; \mu, k) &= \frac{\Gamma(y+k)}{\Gamma(k)\cdot y!} \left(\frac{\mu}{\mu+k}\right)^y\left(\frac{k}{\mu+k}\right)^k \\
  &=\exp\left(y \log \left(\frac{\mu}{\mu+k}\right) + k\left(\frac{k}{\mu+k}\right) + \log\left(\frac{\Gamma(y+k)}{\Gamma(k)\cdot y!}\right)\right),\quad \mu>0,\  k>0
\end{aligned}
\] When the parameter \(k\) is fixed (known), then \(\{f(.;\mu, k), \mu>0\}\) is an exponential dispersion family, with

canonical parameter \(\theta = \log \left(\frac{\mu}{\mu+k}\right)\),
cumulant function \(b(\theta) = -k\log(1-\text{e}^\theta)\),
dispersion parameter \(\phi = 1\).

However, the full family \(\{f(.;\mu, k), \mu>0, k> 0\}\) is unfortunately not an exponential dispersion family.
It is therefore possible with standard methods to get a maximum likelihood estimate for \(\theta\), and thus for \(\mu\), if we know \(k\), but not necessarily to estimate \(\theta\) and \(k\) simultaneously.

title: The truth about the negative binomial distribution and glm.nb
section: Iterative solution to fit a negative binomial glm with two parameters, \(\mu\) and \(k\)
text:
Iterative solution to fit a negative binomial glm with two parameters, \(\mu\) and \(k\)
The most common way to fit a NB glm is iteratively fitting \(\mu\) and \(k\). In the model, \(k\) is assumed to be a constant that does not depend on the explanatory variables. This is also implemented in the glm.nb function from the MASS package.

first make an initial guess \(k_0\) for \(k\),
then iterate until changes from one iteration to the next are sufficiently small:

fit a NB glm with known \(k\) from the previous iteration (or start value), and get the estimate for \(\mu\) from there
then solve the maximum likelihood equations for \(k\), using the latest estimate for \(\mu\) like a known constant.


Maximum likelihood fitting one parameter while replacing the others by estimates is called maximum profile likelihood
The canonical link function, \(g(\mu)=\log \left(\frac{\mu}{\mu+k}\right)\), turns out to be problematic with this procedure, because it depends on both \(\mu\) and \(k\), which can add to instability and non-convergence. Therefore, traditionally other link functions are preferred that only depend on \(\mu\).
A recent paper by Miranda-Soberanis and Lee (2023): Two-parameter link functions, with applications to negative binomial, Weibull and quantile regression (Computational Statistics, Vol 38, 1463–1485) sheds more light on the problematics of the canonical link function in the NB model.

title: The truth about the negative binomial distribution and glm.nb
section: Does a maximum likelihood estimate always exist at all?
text:
Does a maximum likelihood estimate always exist at all?
Negative binomial distributions with fixed parameter \(k\) form an exponential family, thus we can be sure to find a unique maximum likelihood estimate for \(\mu\). However, for the two-parameter family NB(\(k\), \(\mu\)), not all samples yield a maximum likelihood estimate. For the Pascal distributions (where \(k\) is an integer), it has already been conjectured by Anscombe (1950, page 367) that a maximum likelihood estimator exists if and only if the sample mean is smaller than the sample variance (the latter with divisor \(n\), not \(n-1\)). The conditions have been made more precise in later papers. Anscombe suggests to set \(\hat{k}=\infty\) in the cases where the maximum likelihood estimator for \(k\) does not exist, and thus assume a Poisson distribution.
You can read more about that interesting problem in the 2019 paper “On computing maximum likelihood estimates for the negative binomial distribution” by Bandara, Gill and Mitra (Statistics & Probability Letters, 148, 54-58).

title: The truth about the negative binomial distribution and glm.nb
text:
R details (package MASS) and experiments

family negative.binomial
The R library MASS includes a family negative.binomial for use with the glm function. In the functions for negative binomial models, the parameter \(k\) is called theta. Maybe you can think of it as written as \(\vartheta\), not to confound it with the canonical parameter.
If family = negative.binomial is used in a call to glm, it will use the log-link function as default, not the canonical link. The canonical link for the negative binomial, \(g(\mu)=\log(\frac{\mu}{\mu+k})\) is is not implemented. Alternatives to the log link are the identity link, and the square root link sqrt.
Try if it retrieves \(\mu\) as the sample mean of a simple iid random sample:

👉 generate the random variables from a Poisson distribution instead of a negative binomial, and fit a glm with \(k=2, 10, 100, 10000\). What happens with the AIC?






For \(k\to\infty\), the negative binomial converges to a Poisson distribution with same mean. This can be explained by the underlying Gamma distribution that controls the parameter of the Poisson distribution: it gets more and more concentrated. To understand the code below, recall that the parameters of the Gamma distribution in the negative binomial model are shape = \(k\) and scale = \(\mu/k\).








function glm.nb
Function glm.nb implements the iterative algorithm sketched above. It has one caveat: if the sample mean is larger than the variance, the algorithm does not converge, but will stop after a given number of iterations (iteration limit reached), and return a large value for \(\hat{k}\). It usually gives a warning, which I suppressed in the code below to avoid a cluttered output.

title: The truth about the negative binomial distribution and glm.nb
section: Likelihood ratio test of the Poisson null hypothesis vs NB
text:
Likelihood ratio test of the Poisson null hypothesis vs NB
It has been suggested to use a likelihood ratio test of Poisson distribution against negative binomial distribution to check for overdispersion, while correcting for the cases where the maximum likelihood estimate does not exist.
The log likelihood ratio statistic is given as
\[
  G_{\text{Pois-NB}}(\boldsymbol{y}) = -2 \left(\ell_{\text{Poisson}}(\hat\mu;\boldsymbol{y}) -\ell_{\text{NegBinom}}(\hat\mu, \hat{k};\boldsymbol{y})\right)
\]
In cases where the sample variance is smaller than the sample mean, we get \(G(\boldsymbol{y}) = 0\), or a very small nominal value.
Let \[
  D(\boldsymbol{Y}) = \frac {s_n^2(\boldsymbol{Y}) }{\overline{Y}},\quad {\overline{Y}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i,\quad s_n^2(\boldsymbol{Y})=
  \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i-\overline{Y})^2.
\] Claim 1: if \({\boldsymbol{Y}}\) is an i.i.d. sample from a Poisson distribution, then conditioned on \(D(\boldsymbol{Y}) > 1)\), the statistics \(G_{\text{Pois-NB}}(\boldsymbol{Y})\) is asymptotically \(\chi^2\) distributed with \(df=1\) degrees of freedom, \[
G_{\text{Pois-NB}}(\boldsymbol{Y}\mid D(\boldsymbol{Y}>1)) \mathrel{\dot{\sim}}\chi^2_1.
\]
Claim 2: if \({\boldsymbol{Y}}\) is an i.i.d. sample from a Poisson distribution, then \[
P(D(\boldsymbol{Y}) > 1)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} \frac{1}{2}.
\]
In the cases where we get no maximum likelihood estimate, we have \(G_{\text{Pois-NB}}(\boldsymbol{Y}\mid D(\boldsymbol{Y}\leq1))=0\), or something close to zero, due to numerical effects, because we would actually fit a Poisson distribution under the NB model. If Claim 2 can be taken to be approximately correct, we would not reject the null hypothesis in 50% of all samples, just because we cannot fit a NB model. In the other 50%, we would obtain a \(\chi^2_1\) distributed statistic, given Claim 1 is applicable. If we bluntly calculate the \(p\)-value as \(p=1-F_{\chi^2_1}(G_{\text{Pois-NB}})\), we would get a very conservative test.
It is therefore suggested to calculate the \(p\)-value as \[
  p_{\text{Pois-NB}}(\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-F_{\chi^2_1}(G_{\text{Pois-NB}}(\boldsymbol{y})\right)
\]
The following code explores Claims 1 and 2. Notice the fantastically convenient function logLik 😊
