title: Binary Data: Analysis, Modelling
text:
Background idea
It is natural in many cases to assume that the Bernoulli outcome \(Y_j\) is determined by a latent random variable \(Z_j\).
The outcome \(Y_j\) is positive if and only if \(Z_j\) exceeds a critical threshold, which can be defined to be zero (\(0\)). Thus,
\[
  Y_j = \begin{cases}
  1,& Z_j > 0\\
  0,& Z_j \leq 0
  \end{cases}.
\]
The variable \(Z_j\) itself depends linearly on the covariate vector \(\mathbf{x}_j\), and a random offset \(\varepsilon_j\sim F\), \[
Z_j=\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\gamma} +\varepsilon_j\cdot\sigma
\]
\(F\) is the tolerance distribution.

title: Binary Data: Analysis, Modelling
section: Link function in the latent variable model
text:
Link function in the latent variable model
Mean of \(Y\) is \(\mathrm{E}\,Y=\pi\). Let \(F\) be the tolerance distribution, i.e. the distribution of \(\varepsilon\).
\[\begin{aligned}
\pi &= \mathrm{P}(Y=1) = \mathrm{P}(Z>0)\\
& =\mathrm{P}(\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\gamma} + \varepsilon\sigma > 0)\\
& =\mathrm{P}(\varepsilon > - \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\gamma} / \sigma)\qquad (\text{write }
\boldsymbol{\beta}:=\boldsymbol{\gamma} / \sigma)\\
& =1 - F( - \underbrace{\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\eta})
\end{aligned}\]
Thus, the link function corresponding to tolerance distribution \(F\) is found by inverting \(\pi = 1-F(-\eta)\), namely
\[
g(\pi) = \eta = -F^{-1}(1-\pi)
\]

shortcut: symmetric tolerance distribution
If \(F\) is symmetric around \(0\) then \[
\pi  =1 - F( - \eta) = F(\eta)
\]
thus the link function is \[
  g(\pi) = F^{-1}(\pi)
\]

title: Examples for approximate confidence intervals
section: normal approximation confidence interval for exponentials
text:
normal approximation confidence interval for exponentials
In the example (Davison, 4.24), the Wald confidence interval for exponentials was derived to be limited by \(\bar{y} \pm z_{0.025}n^{-1/2}\bar{y}\) (with confidence level 0.95):
The exponential distribution with density \(f(y; \theta) =\frac{1}{\theta}\mathrm{e}^{-y/\theta}, \quad y>0, \theta>0\) gives log likelihood \[
\ell(\theta; y_1,\dots,y_n) = -n\log\theta -\sum_{i=1}^n y_i/\theta.
\] Score function is thus \[
  U(\theta) = -\frac{n}{\theta} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i}{\theta^2}
\] From \(U(\hat\theta)=0\) we find \(\hat\theta = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i =\bar{y}\). The observed information and expected is thus \[
  J(\theta) = -\frac{d U(\theta)}{d\theta} = -\frac{n}{\theta^2}+2\frac{n\bar{y}}{\theta^3},\quad I(\theta)=\mathrm{E}J(\theta)=-\frac{n}{\theta^2}+2\frac{n\theta}{\theta^3}=\frac{n}{\theta^2}.
\] For the approximate confidence interval, we need \(J(\hat\theta)\) or \(I(\hat\theta)\), which in this example is the same, \(I(\hat\theta) = J(\hat\theta)=n/\bar{y}^2\)
We thus get the limits of the approximate confidence interval with (nominal) coverage \(1-2\alpha\) as \[
\hat\theta \pm z_{1-\alpha} I(\hat\theta)^{-1/2} = \bar{y}  \pm z_{1-\alpha}\frac{\bar{y}}{\sqrt{n}} = \bar{y}\left(1 \pm z_{1-\alpha}/\sqrt{n}\right)
\] Implementing this confidence interval:

For exponential (\(\theta\)) distributed \(Y_1,\dots, Y_n\), the sum has a Gamma distribution with shape parameter \(n\) and rate parameter \(1/\theta\). The confidence interval is found from \[
\begin{aligned}
&P(F_{\Gamma(n, 1/\theta)}^{-1}(\alpha/2) < n\bar{Y}\leq P(F_{\Gamma(n, 1/\theta)}^{-1}(1-\alpha/2) )\\& \qquad= P(F_{\Gamma(n, 1)}^{-1}(\alpha/2) < n\bar{Y}/\theta\leq P(F_{\Gamma(n, 1)}^{-1}(1-\alpha/2) ).
\end{aligned}
\]

Exercise 2
Try to derive and implement the exact confidence interval as a function confint_exponential and check out if it works as supposed.

title: Experiments with likelihood curves
text:
This little example illustrates the random nature of likelihood functions: you can consider them as a transformation of the (random) data.
Look at the exponential distribution with rate parameter \(\theta\). It has density \[
f(y; \theta) = {\theta} \exp(-\theta y).
\]
The log likelihood function from a dataset of size \(n\) is \[
\ell(\theta) = n (\log\theta - \theta\bar{y}).
\]
The maximum likelihood estimator for \(\theta\) is \[\hat\theta = 1 / \bar{y},\] and from that we get the log relative likelihood, \(\log RL(\theta) = \ell(\theta) -\ell(\hat\theta)\).
